sections.title: Whole quick matches: 10 hands
sections.text: This is the format on the site: 10 hands, both players starting every hand with 20 big blinds, and the winner is whoever has won more chips. Matches were played in pairs with the same cards and the seats swapped. A draw counts as half a win. Ten hands carry a lot of luck, so even a much stronger player loses some matches.

sections.title: Earlier quick-match format: first to 3,000 chips
sections.text: The site used this format before the 10-hand match. Blinds rose every 5 hands and one all-in could end a match in two or three hands, so it carried even more luck.

sections.title: Slumbot: the independent test
sections.text: Slumbot won the 2018 Annual Computer Poker Competition and has a public API. It is the only opponent here I did not write. These matches are 200 big blinds deep with no duplicate deals, so variance is far higher than in the tables above. The all-in adjusted rows score hands where both players were all-in before the river at their expected value over the remaining cards, a standard way to remove some of the luck. They use the same hands. The first match solved the turn for 20 iterations and the river for 150, which turned out to leave the Expert betting the turn far too often. The rematch used 300 and 600, the most the site runs while you take your time, and the longer-trained 200bb blueprint, so it reflects both fixes together.
sections.note: For scale, published wins against Slumbot run from Modicum at +11 ± 5 mbb/hand and ReBeL at +45 ± 5 to Supremus at +176 ± 44, all over far larger samples and with far more compute. A true edge as large as the rematch result would be surprising, so the real margin is most likely smaller. The fair reading is that the Expert now holds its own against Slumbot, not that it is stronger.

sections.title: Local Best Response: how exploitable is it?
sections.text: LBR is told the exact strategy, then attacks it greedily, assuming the hand checks down afterwards. If LBR won, that would prove a minimum amount the bot can be exploited by. The table shows how much the bot won against LBR, as in the ReBeL paper: positive means the attack failed. That is evidence, not proof, that the bot is hard to exploit.
sections.note: For scale, ReBeL beat LBR by 881 ± 94 and DeepStack by 383 ± 112, when LBR had to call through preflop and flop at 200bb (the "turn" rows here).

sections.title: Speed in the browser
sections.text: Measured in Chrome. Preflop and flop decisions took 17 ms and 10 ms on average. Turn solves are capped at about 1.5 s and river solves at about 0.7 s. The throttled rows are a rough stand-in for phones, not tests on real phones.
